header.title: Canon vel Constitutio 'Qualiter Ecclesiastici Gradus Custodiantur': AI translation (Claude)
header.author: SS Silvester I
header.source: Translated by Claude (claude-opus-5-5, Anthropic) from the library's tmp90.tmp90.opp-lat1, from Open Greek and Latin's Patrologia Latina (CC BY-SA 4.0), one English line for each line of the original. The whole work is translated. It was chosen because no English translation of it could be found.
header.statement: An AI-generated translation of the whole work, checked against the original by a second AI only in samples. No specialist has reviewed it.
header.availability: CC BY-SA 4.0, as its source requires: credit Open Greek and Latin's Patrologia Latina and this AI translation, and share adaptations under the same licence.

notes.urn:cts:latinLit:tmp90.tmp90.opp-lat1.he: The Latin of this forged text is very corrupt and often ungrammatical, especially in ch. 1 (anacoluthic sentences beginning 'Silvester igitur…' and 'Hos omnes…'), ch. 2 and ch. 4; the translation follows the words as closely as sense allows. 'patris Rinocororis' read as 'partis Rhinocorurae' (region of Rhinocorura); uncertain. 'probo' in ch. 2 taken in the sense 'condemn' (as the context requires; perhaps for 'reprobo'). 'Jobinianum' in ch. 2 is evidently the same figure later called Victorinus; the confusion is in the text. 'indicio' read as 'judicio', 'Angustorum' as 'Augustorum', 'damnabit' as 'damnavit', 'Mojorianus' as 'Majorianus'. 'regiae ecclesiae non vaticinentur' is obscure; 'vaticinentur' perhaps for 'vacillent', rendered 'waver'. In ch. 4 the division of the revenues is garbled (four parts, then halves). 'Martia-' in the list is cut off in the edition. In the toc, 'det poenitentiam' may mean 'receive/do penance'.
notes.urn:cts:latinLit:tmp90.tmp90.opp-lat1.1a: The Latin of this forgery is extremely ungrammatical throughout; the translation follows it literally and some constructions are guesses. 6.1: 'pallia linostimia' (linen-wool cloth) sense uncertain. 1a.10.1 and 1b.10.1: the age 'seventy-two years' is as in the text; the first edition's 'probabitur judicium, pudicitia vero, ut in...' and the second's 'judici a pudicitia vera, aut in septuaginta annis' are both garbled; the first has 'verum Christum' (true Christ) where the second has 'virum Christum' (husband Christ). 1b.1.1: 'uno examen articulo sanctitatis' is obscure; 'Rinocoruris' taken as Rhinocorura. The count of 6 deacons and 'diaconi omnes ducenti octoginta quatuor' in 2a.1 (284 = number of bishops) are as printed. 1b.2.1: 'probo' taken in the sense 'I condemn/prove guilty' given the context; Jovianus in the charge is replaced by Hippolytus in the condemnation, as in the text. 1b.4.1: 'quarta pars' where the first edition has 'primam partem'. 2a.1: only five deacons are named though seven regions are made; 'praeter synodi' read as 'apart from the synod'. Scanning slips corrected silently (El = Et, Subdianonus, plublico, oro = ore).
notes.urn:cts:latinLit:tmp90.tmp90.opp-lat1.2a: The stretch gives two parallel recensions of the Second Session and chapters XI–XX (the two manuscripts printed side by side by Crabbe), both badly corrupt; translated as they stand. In 2a.11.1 'privaretur doctrinae' (deprived of teaching) is evidently a corruption of 'probaretur' (be proved), as the 2b text reads; it is rendered literally there. 'Finctus est enim' (XIII) is obscure, perhaps for 'fictus' (feigned) or 'functus'. In 2a.17.1 'triduo' (three days) against 2b 'duo' (two). In 2a.12.1 'Matth. ultimo' is an editorial reference to Matthew 28 that has crept into the text. 'Curia a cruore' is a false etymology. 'Aspersit' (sprinkled) is likely corrupt for 'sparsit' or similar (distributed). 'meamus' in the final line is read as 'doctissimus' or similar ('most learned'); the reading is uncertain. 'Crabb.' is Petrus Crabbe; 'Constant.' is taken as Pierre Coustant.
Several evident scanning errors were read as intended: 'manse Malo anni 424' as mense Maio anni 324; 'Victorum' as Victorinus; 'meae latina' as mere latina; 'solem' as solent; 'collari' as collati; 'fictilia ... memorari' as [canones] ... memorati; 'parenti' taken as 'author'. In VII, 'sumat' is unclear (perhaps assereret/sumeret), rendered 'held'. In VIII, 'Calistus Jovianus' is taken as two names (Callistus and Jovianus/Jovinianus); 'episcopi partis et Rinocoruris' is obscure, perhaps a corruption of a phrase naming Egypt, rendered literally.

Line 13: 'in fictori nemo potest' read as 'inficiari nemo potest' (no one can deny); 'Columbam' as Columbanus; 'don sine' as 'non sine'; 'Alii jam ratione' as 'Alia jam ratione'. Line 1a: 'successorem Zozimi ad successores Patrocli' read as plural 'successores Zozimi'; the sentence is somewhat elliptical. 'V. c.' taken as vir clarissimus.

Line 3.2.2a: 'Austudunensis' read as Augustodunensis (Autun); Retitius is Reticius, bishop of Autun. Line 3.3.1a: the text reads 'ubique non misisse manifestum est' ('it is clear [we] have not sent'), which contradicts the sense; translated as 'nos misisse' ('we have sent'), the evident reading. The numbered marks (1)-(9) are editorial footnote references and are omitted. Line 3.3.2a: '(Add. quinta)' is an editorial insertion in the printed text.

nodes.text: CANON OR CONSTITUTION OF SILVESTER, BISHOP OF THE CITY OF ROME,
AND OF THE LORD CONSTANTINE AUGUSTUS, ON HOW THE ECCLESIASTICAL GRADES, AND RELIGION, ARE TO BE KEPT.
(Conc. vol. I, col. 1544.)

Headings of the canons. I. On the assembly of bishops and deacons.—II. On the condemnation of Callistus, Victorinus and Hippolytus.—III. That through the several grades no one may bring a charge [against a superior].—IV. That four parts be made of the revenues of the Church.—V. That no presbyter make chrism.—VI. On the deacons of the parishes, and the cardinal deacons of the city of Rome.—VII. That from subdeacon down to lector, all be subject to the cardinal deacon of the city of Rome.—VIII. That no subdeacon pass to marriage.—IX. No lector, no acolyte may touch the sacred vessels.—X. No bishop may bless a consecrated virgin for married union.—XI. That no one from the lay state be raised from the rank of acolyte up to the episcopate except through the several grades.—XII. No one may give penance unless [he is] forty years old.—XIII. On a certain mystery.—XIV. No one may receive the testimony of a cleric against a layman.—XV. No one may examine a cleric in public.—XVI. That no cleric, deacon or presbyter enter a court on account of his own case.—XVII. That no one strike a sinning cleric with blows.—XVIII. That no deacon bring a charge against a presbyter.—XIX. That no presbyter take a wife from the day of his priesthood.—XX. That no one judge the first see of justice.
FIRST SESSION.
First edition. CHAPTER 1.

Constitution of canons, on how grade and religion are to be kept, by Silvester, bishop of the city of Rome, [and] the lord Constantine. At the time when many nobles were rejoicing that Constantine had been baptized by Silvester, bishop of the city of Rome, and cleansed of leprosy, for the benefit he had received from our Lord Jesus Christ through Bishop Silvester he began to preach the Lord Jesus Christ wholeheartedly and to confess his benefits. So Silvester, bishop of the city of Rome, gathering his brothers, his fellow presbyters and fellow bishops and deacons, Roman citizens, and since mother Church had borne a most dear son, Constantine. Wholeheartedly therefore Silvester, bishop of the city of Rome, desires to set his own [people] in order, and to suckle her sons often, and to lay out the grades of her order and custom. He gathered the whole synod of bishops with the counsel of the Augustus and his mother, and had [it] prepared in the city of Rome in the Baths of Domitian, which are now called the Baths of Trajan. He gathered into the bosom of his see 284 bishops, to whom the Augustus Constantine ordered vehicles and provisions to be supplied in every place, and another 57 bishops of the region of Rhinocorura, whose signed document is set out in their council, and 62 presbyters of the city of Rome, and deacons [and] acolytes made by his counsel, 22 exorcists, 90 lectors of the city of Rome, of whom those present were heard. [Also] 14 notaries of the Church, who, taking up the acts of various martyrs, recounted them in order. All these, too, while he gathered [them] for examination in one point of holiness in the aforesaid baths, yet so that no layman should appear to preside.
There follow 139 bishops from the city of Rome or not far from it.

Castus, Cyprus, Petrus, Abundius, Severinus, Lucianus, Capax, Herculanus, Joannes, Himilus, Andreas, Petrus, Renovatus, Cresconius, Ambrosius, Lucas, Hermogenianus, Augustus, Felix, Barbarus, Secundinus, Citonatus, Reparatus, Gaudentius, Sebastianus, Graeces (otherwise Cresces), Renatus, Hirenaeus, Laurentius, Valerianus, Botudorus, Leo, Abundantius, Almachius, Honestosus, Victor, Plenus, Delphinus, Amabilis, Paulus, Constantius, Sixtus, Concordius, Nepotianus, Bedandulus, Deutherius, Amabilis, Syrus, Quadratus, Mirabilis, Audacius, Turcilianus, Joannes, Marcus, Fidelis, Symmachus, Probianus, Asellus, Crispinus, Rusticus, Faustus, Turdus, Majorianus, Jobianus, Exonosus, Sanctulus, Coricosus, Nepus, Tiburtius, Petrus, Sylvestrianus, Turturanus, Leontius, Anastasius, Agapitus, Verustimilus, Asellus, Jacobus, Felicissimus, Quadratus, Alexander, Philippus, Exuperantius, Hypolitus (Hippolytus), Jordianus, Archidamus, Lollius, Martia-, Caritosus, Concordius, Januarius, Felicianus, Redus, Auxibus, Timotheus, Bonifacius, Tranquillinus, Calbulus, Sixtus, Catellus, Epiphanes, Victor, Habet Deum, Contentus, Apronianus, Probus, Repostibus, Paulus, Fidelissimus, Homobonus, Luminosus, Vitalis, Carpilio, Volusianus, Petrus, Probinus, Honestosus, Ariston, Bacanda, Petrus, Marinus, Priscillianus, Carito, Gattus, Januarius, Caecilius, Epiphanius, Laurentius, Humanianus, Urbanus, Micinus, Caecilius, Priscus, Tiburtius, Nonnonus, Anthimus, Agapitus, Vindemius.
And these are from Greece.

Petrus, Anastasius, Hermes, Nicostratus, Quodvultdeus, Vitalis, Renatus, Vinulus, Andriphorus, Hirenaeus, Olympius, Demeter, Theodolus, Anastasius, Thespias, Firminus, Cleopatris, Honorius, Simplex, Exitiosus, Joannes, Timotheus, Hermes, Paulus, Metronius, Stephanus, Alexander, Constantinus, Andreas, Exuperantius, Firmus, Quirillianus, Anastasius, Hermogenius, Severus, Aconcius, Thomas, Joannes, Caecilianus, Theodolus, Theophilus, Prispilius, Festus, Almacus, Andecius, Concordius, Deutherinnus, Thomas, Quadratus, Timotheus, Potestas, Andreas, Philippus, Thomas, Victorinus, Severianus, Domanicus, Eulogius, Demeter, Nepotianus, Albinus, Petrus, Joannes, Exuperius, Theodolus, Joannes, Exuperantius, Sebastianus, Theodorus, Claudius, Demetrianus, Rufinus, Spes in Deo, Reparatus, Petrus, Asellus, Archanus, Eufemius, Crisolatus, Lazarus, Leo, Anthimus, Andreas, Catharon, Vultibus, Anastasius, Hermes, Sempervivus, Titus, Orifensis, Epiphanius, Anastasius, Leo, Ultius, Fortunatus, Caecilianus, Nicostratus, Audax, Joannes, Rufinus, Honorius, Felix, Petronius, Andreas, Requisitus, Bacauda, Terfilius, Zenon, Caritosus, Majoranus, Leo, Hermes, Demeter, Andreas, Spes in Deo, Timotheus, Jacobus, Zenon, Quadratus, Fusilis, Marcus, Paulinus, Oyfensis, Concordius, Priscus, Herculanus, Leoninus, Androtilus, Eufimius, Squiro, Martinus, Anastasius.

When all these had come to the synod, and others whose signed document and reputation for holiness had gone before, they sat down within sight of the same aforesaid baths. All the Roman presbyters and deacons, and the clergy and the grades following, stood behind the bishops. For no one sat in that place except the bishops alone, and Bishop Silvester, pontiff of the city of Rome. Calpurnius was also there, first a pagan and afterwards a Christian, prefect of the city. And Silvester, bishop of the city of Rome, spoke this address: Hear me, brothers and fellow bishops, and the whole order of the Roman Church, for it is good that the Church should have fixed curtains, so that the royal churches may not waver, but that she may be firm, and shut the door because of the persecutor, and have a firm wall from which to fight off her adversaries.
CHAPTER II.

I speak what is known, and I condemn Callistus and Victorinus, who by their own judgement made a creature, and Jovinianus, who in his arrogance said [Easter was to be kept] not by the month, but on the tenth day before the Kalends of May. For I (as the law records) commit the matter to your judgement, that these three be brought in, [and that] first, by the judgement concerning Callistus, the sentence condemning [him] be confirmed, Callistus who so taught himself Sabellianism that by his own judgement he held the Trinity to be one person. For since he did not make Father, Son and Holy Spirit equal; [and] Victorinus, so chiefly a prelate of religion, who in his fierceness affirmed to men whatever he wished, and declared the Easter cycles false, so that what he laid down, that [Easter] be kept on the tenth day before the Kalends of May, may by your word, as the truth has it, be stopped, and be condemned by your judgement, and the authority of our sons the Augusti may go before in condemning Bishop Victorinus. And he condemned Hippolytus the deacon, a Valentinian, and Callistus, who in his arrogance divided the Trinity, and Bishop Victorinus, who, ignorant of the reckoning of the moon, broke down the truth under the obstinacy of his own judgement; and in the presence of the aforesaid bishops and presbyters he condemned Hippolytus, Victorinus and Callistus, and gave them anathema, and condemned them [to exile] outside their cities.
CHAPTER III.

Afterwards he set up grades in the bosom of the synod, so that no presbyter against a bishop, no deacon against a presbyter, no subdeacon against a deacon, no exorcist against an acolyte, no lector against an exorcist, no doorkeeper against a lector may bring any accusation; and a prelate shall not be condemned except by seventy-two [witnesses]; nor shall the highest prelate be judged by anyone, since it is written: The disciple is not above the master. A presbyter shall not be condemned except by forty-four testimonies. A cardinal deacon bound to the city of Rome shall not be condemned except by thirty-six. A subdeacon, acolyte, exorcist, lector, [shall not be condemned] except (as it is written) by seven testimonies [of men] having sons and a wife, wholly preaching Christ, as the mystical truth is given.
CHAPTER IV.

I remind you, my colleagues, of the record that four parts be made of the revenues of the church, and that the church should exact the first part: one part for the pontiff with the brothers who are to be relieved, half for the church, half for the presbyters and deacons with all the clergy, or for strangers. He laid down this order: that if any of the clergy or the presbyters of any place whatever, which is a common thing, should pass from this world, and had no partner of his own kin, whatever his poverty possessed he should bestow on the church, and from it four parts should be made, as has been said.
CHAPTER V.
Silvester, bishop of the city of Rome, also laid down in a clear voice that no presbyter should make chrism, saying that Christ is to be named from chrism.
CHAPTER VI.

That there should be no more deacons, nor any greater number, through the examination of the parishes, than two, and seven cardinal deacons of the city of Rome; on condition, however, that they should wear dalmatics and that *linostimia* palls (linen-and-wool mantles) should cover their left [side].
CHAPTER VII.

And thus Silvester said in a clear voice to his fellow bishops, that from the subdeacon down to the reader all should be subject to the cardinal deacon of the city of Rome, showing him honour only in the Church; but to the pontiff the presbyters, subdeacons, deacons, acolytes, exorcist [and] reader [are to be subject], showing obedience in every place, whether in public or in the bosom of the Church, to the pontiff alone.
CHAPTER VIII.
We command that none of the subdeacons pass over to marriage, lest he presume [to do so] by some transgression.
CHAPTER IX.

No reader or doorkeeper should touch the sacred vessels; no acolyte should hand on to another a sacred thing [received] from a presbyter, but should only carry what the priest places on him, blessed by his mouth.
CHAPTER X.

Also, no bishop should seek to have a consecrated virgin blessed with a marital [blessing], unless he has proved her to be established at seventy-two years of age, where the judgement shall be proved; and as for chastity, that [having kept it] up to seventy-two years, seeking the true Christ, with chastity preserved, with anointed head, she be led in to the nuptials of Christ, wearing the veil of the head, not of the heart. And the bishops named above subscribed to this, Silvester, bishop of the city of Rome, proclaiming [it]. And last subscribed Calpurnus, prefect of the city. And Constantine Augustus subscribed, with his mother Helena Augusta. Then he gave a prayer, sitting in the same place, and they departed.
Second edition. CHAPTER I.

At the same time, when many nobles rejoiced that Constantine had been baptised by Silvester of the city of Rome and had been cleansed of leprosy, through this benefit, which he received from the Lord Jesus Christ through Silvester the bishop, he began wholeheartedly to preach the Lord Jesus Christ and to confess his benefits. Silvester, therefore, bishop of the city of Rome, gathering his brothers, fellow presbyters and fellow bishops, and his deacons, Roman citizens. And since mother Church had borne a most dear son, Constantine, therefore Silvester, bishop of the city of Rome, with his own [clergy], desired to set her in order, and to nurse her sons frequently, and to lay out the grades of her order and her customs. He gathered the whole synod of bishops with the counsel of the Augustus and his mother, and had [it] prepared in the city of Rome within the Baths of Domitian, which are now called [the Baths] of Trajan. He gathered in the bosom of his see two hundred and eighty-four bishops, to whom Constantine Augustus ordered carriages and provisions to be supplied, and another 57 bishops of the region of Rhinocorura, whose signed document is set out in their council; one hundred and forty-two presbyters of the city of Rome, and 6 deacons, 6 subdeacons, forty-five acolytes made at his council, 22 exorcists, ninety readers of the city of Rome, whose parents heard [the proceedings] in person; 14 notaries of the Church, who, taking up the acts of various martyrs, related them in order. All these, moreover, he gathered by one examination at the point of holiness in the baths mentioned above, but in such a way that no layman was seen present.

When all these had come into the synod, and the signed document of some had circulated, and the reputation for holiness, they sat in the same view of the baths mentioned above. All the Roman presbyters, deacons, and clergy, or the grades following, stood behind the bishops. For no one sat in that place except only the bishops and Silvester the bishop, pontiff of the city of Rome. For Calphurnius too was there, who was first a pagan and afterwards a Christian, and prefect of the city. Silvester, bishop of the city of Rome, speaks this address: 'Hear me, brothers and fellow bishops, and the whole order of the Roman Church, since it is good that the Church should have fixed curtains, so that the royal church may not be shaken, but be firm, and shut the door against the persecutor, and have a firm wall from which to fight off its adversaries.
CHAPTER II.

I speak of what is known, and I condemn Callistus and Victorinus, who by their own will made a creature, and Jovianus, who in his arrogance said that Easter does not come on its own day nor in its own month, but [is] to be kept on the tenth day before the Kalends of May. For I, as the law records, commit the matter to your judgement, that these three be brought in; and first, that the examination of Callistus by [your] will be confirmed to condemn [him], who so taught himself, Callistus, as a Sabellian, that by his own will he takes the Trinity to be one person, not making the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit co-equal. As for Victorinus, chiefly prelate [and] high priest of the region, who in his ferocity [did] whatever he wished to men, and proclaimed false cycles of Easter, so that what he laid down, that [it] be kept on the tenth day before the Kalends of May, may by your word, as the truth has it, be annulled and by your judgement condemned, and the authority of our sons may hasten to condemn bishop Victorinus.' And they all came in, so that they might be condemned by his word in judgement. He condemned Hippolytus the deacon, a Valentinian, and Callistus, who in his arrogance divided the Trinity, and bishop Victorinus, who, ignorant of the reckoning of the moon, broke the truth by the obstinacy of his own will. And in the presence of the bishops mentioned above and of the presbyters and the other grades, he condemned Hippolytus, Victorinus and Callistus. And he gave them anathema, and condemned them [to be] outside their cities.
CHAPTER III.

Afterwards he set out the grades in the midst of the synod: that no presbyter against a bishop, no deacon against a presbyter, no subdeacon against a deacon, no acolyte against a subdeacon, no exorcist against an acolyte, no reader against an exorcist, no doorkeeper against a reader, no layman should bring any accusation. And a prelate shall not be condemned except by seventy-two [witnesses], nor shall the supreme prelate be judged by anyone, since it is written: The disciple is not above the master. A presbyter shall not be condemned except by forty-four testimonies. A deacon established as cardinal of the city shall not be condemned except by 36. A subdeacon, acolyte, exorcist, reader, [not] except (as it is written) by seven testimonies, [of men] having sons and wives and wholly preaching Christ. Thus is the mystical truth given.
CHAPTER IV.

I remind you, my colleagues, of the safeguard, and that four parts be made of the revenues of the church, and that the fourth part be exacted from the church: one part for the pontiffs, half for the brothers for relieving the churches, half for the presbyters and deacons with all the clergy, and for strangers. He laid down this order: that if any of the clergy or the presbyters of any place whatever, which is a common thing, should pass from this world, if he had no partner of his own kin, whatever his poverty possessed he should bestow on the church, and from it four parts should be made, as has been said above.
CHAPTER V.
For Silvester, bishop of the city of Rome, laid down in a clear voice that no presbyter should make chrism, saying that Christ is named from chrism.
CHAPTER VI.
And that there should be no more deacons, nor any greater number, through the examination of the parishes, than two, and seven cardinal deacons of the city of Rome.
CHAPTER VII.

Thus, however, Silvester said in a clear voice to his fellow bishops, [that] from the subdeacon down to the reader all should be subject to the cardinal deacon of the city of Rome, showing [honour] only in the Church. But to the pontiff the presbyters, deacons, subdeacons, acolytes, exorcists [and] reader [are subject], showing obedience in every place, whether in public or in the bosom of the Church, to the pontiff alone.
CHAPTER VIII.
We command that none of the subdeacons pass over to marriage, lest he incur some transgression.
CHAPTER IX.

No reader or doorkeeper should touch the sacred vessels; no acolyte should hand on to another a sacred thing [received] from a presbyter, but should only carry what the priest places on him, blessed by his mouth.
CHAPTER X.

Also, no bishop should seek to bless a consecrated virgin for marital union, unless he has proved her to be established at seventy-two years of age. There she shall be proved by the judge by true chastity, or, seeking the husband Christ for seventy years, with chastity preserved, with anointed head, let her be led in to the nuptials of Christ, wearing the veil of the head, not of the heart. And the bishops named above subscribed to this, Silvester, bishop of the city of Rome, proclaiming [it]. And last subscribed Calphurnius, prefect of the city. Constantine Augustus subscribed with his mother Helena Augusta. Then he gave a prayer, sitting in the same place, and they departed.
SECOND SESSION.

On another day all the presbyters of the city of Rome came, and all the deacons, two hundred and eighty-four, to the Baths of Domitian, which are now [called] of Trajan, and he sat on his seat in the same place. There he made seven regions and divided them among the deacons. These deacons were Fabianus, Marcus, Liverius, Archidamus, Julius. He ordained two others, Priscus and Theodorus; the whole [assembly of either] sex, the presbyters, deacons and clergy asked this of Silvester the bishop, that he ordain them. There in the baths he appointed these two, Priscus and Theodorus, as subordinates; he did not ordain or consecrate them, but consecrated [them] in the bosom of the basilica, and established [this] apart from the synod.
CHAPTER XI.

That no one from the lay state should be raised to the rank of acolyte, up to the episcopate, unless he had first been a reader for thirty years. Then for one day an exorcist, and afterwards he should take up the charge of acolyte, and serve in that same order as acolyte for ten years, so that he might receive the charge of subdeacon, and he should be in the subdiaconate for five years; then, being established, he should attain the rank of the diaconate, thirty presbyters requesting an examination, so that he might be a cardinal deacon, because it had been established by the first see that he should serve seven years. For this [is so], that if anyone desired the order of the presbyterate, it should be required thus: that for seven years he should be deprived by the whole Roman clergy of teaching, of birth, of nobility, and of counsel, not seeking plunder from anyone, [and] with clear reputation all the presbyters should declare and confirm [him] firmly, and so they should come to the order of the presbyterate, and serve in that same order three years. And if order, or arrangement, or care of piety or of holiness requires [him] to come to the charge of the episcopate, [it should be] that all the clergy ask that he be ordained by one lasting vote. Which was done thus, and nothing was opposed to the words of Silvester the bishop, but rather they confirmed [them] by prayer. And Silvester, bishop of the city of Rome, said this also: Hear, holy ones and fellow bishops. Let no one hide what seems to him [fit] for justice to rebuke. Then all the bishops answered, and said, crying out with all the presbyters and clergy: In you is justice, and may piety not depart from you, since nothing will be judged by us against the opinion of your sayings, since there is no wisdom unless it has been built on patience. And Silvester the bishop said: Since, if there is no wisdom except in patience, whatever I establish by word, let it be confirmed by your signed document.
CHAPTER XII.
Let no one give penance except to one of forty years asking [for it]: baptism, preaching, give to all, Matthew, last [chapter].
CHAPTER XIII.
Let no one who has not first received the heavenly veil of marriage by the hands of a priest come to the rank of the clerical state. For he is feigned.
CHAPTER XIV.
Let no one receive the testimony of a cleric against a layman.
CHAPTER XV.
Let no one examine any cleric in public, except in church.
CHAPTER XVI.

Let no cleric, or deacon, or presbyter enter a court for any cause of his own, since every court [curia] is named from blood [cruor], and is the sacrifice of idols. But if any cleric enters a court, let him receive anathema, never returning to mother church. But let him not be deprived of communion, on account of the troubled time.
CHAPTER XVII.

Let no one strike any sinning cleric with a beating; let no presbyter, no deacon, no bishop bring a cleric or servant of the church to a beating. But if the case of the cleric so requires, let him be deprived of his rank for three days, so that as penitents they may return to mother Church.
CHAPTER XVIII.
Let no deacon bring a charge of indecency against presbyters.
CHAPTER XIX.

Let no presbyter, from the day he takes up the charge of the presbyterate, take a wife, so that if anyone goes out in neglect [of this], we say he is deprived of his rank for twelve years. But if anyone has acted [against] this present signed document and the public decree, let him be condemned for ever.
CHAPTER XX.

Let no one judge the first see, desiring justice to be tempered; neither by the Augustus, nor by all the clergy, nor by kings, nor by the people shall the judge be judged. And two hundred and eighty-four bishops subscribed, and forty-five presbyters, and five deacons, and the two following, and Constantine Augustus, and his mother Helena. And Silvester, bishop of the city of Rome, fixed this canon, and sprinkled [it] on all the bishops. Done in the Baths of Trajan, on the third day before the Kalends of June, in the third [consulship] of the Lord Constantine Augustus, and Priscus being consul.
SECOND SESSION.

On another day all the presbyters of the city of Rome came, and the deacons, and all the bishops, two hundred and eighty-four, into the Baths of Domitian, which are now [called] of Trajan, and he sat on his seat in the same place. There he made seven regions, and divided them among the deacons. These deacons were Fabianus, Marcus, Liberius, Archidamus, Julius. And he ordained also two others, Priscus and Theodorus. The whole [assembly of either] sex, the presbyters and deacons and clergy asked this of Silvester the bishop, that he ordain them. There in the baths he appointed these two, Priscus and Theodorus, as subordinates; he did not ordain and consecrate them, but consecrated them in the bosom of the basilica, and established [this] apart from the synod.
CHAPTER XI.

That no one from the lay state should be raised to the rank of acolyte, up to the episcopate, unless he had first been a reader for thirty years, then for one day an exorcist, and afterwards he should take up the charge of acolyte, and serve in that same order of acolyte ten years, so that he might receive the charge of subdeacon, and he should be in the subdiaconate five years. Then, being established, he should attain the rank of the diaconate, thirty presbyters requesting an examination, so that he might be a cardinal subdeacon, because it had been established by the first see that he should serve seven years. For this [is so], that if anyone desired the order of presbyter, it should be required thus: that for seven years he should be proved by the whole Roman clergy in teaching, birth, nobility, and counsel, not seeking plunder from anyone; with clear reputation all the presbyters should confirm, declare and confirm [him], and so he should come to the order of the presbyterate, and serve in that same order three years. And if order or arrangement, or care of piety or holiness requires, he should come to the charge of the episcopate, as all the clergy should ask, to ordain [him] by one lasting vote; which was done thus, and the synod opposed nothing to the words of Silvester the bishop, but rather confirmed [them] by prayer. And Silvester, bishop of the city of Rome, said this also: Hear, holy ones and fellow bishops. Let no one hide what might seem to him [fit] for justice to rebuke. All the bishops answered, and said, crying out with all the presbyters and clergy: Justice will conquer, and may [the virtue] of piety not depart from you. Since nothing will be judged by us against the opinion of your sayings, since there is no wisdom unless it has been built on patience. And Silvester the bishop said: Since, if there is no wisdom except in patience, whatever I establish by word, let it be confirmed by your signed document.
CHAPTER XII.
Let no one give penance except to one of forty years asking [for it]. But give baptism to all.
CHAPTER XIII.

Let no one come to the rank of the clerical state unless he has first received the heavenly veil of marriage by the hands of a priest. The testimony of a cleric against a layman [is] not to be admitted. For he is feigned.
CHAPTER XIV.
Let no one receive the testimony of a cleric against a layman.
CHAPTER XV.
Let no one examine any cleric in public, except in church.
CHAPTER XVI.
Let no cleric or deacon, or presbyter enter a court for any cause of his own, since every court [curia] is named from blood [cruor], and is the sacrifice
of idols. Since, if any cleric enters a court, let him receive anathema, never returning to mother church. But let him not be deprived of communion, on account of the troubled time.
CHAPTER XVII.

Let no one strike any sinning cleric with a beating; let no presbyter, no deacon, no bishop bring a cleric or servant of the church to a beating. But if the case of the cleric so requires, let the two be deprived of rank, so that [they return] as penitents to mother Church.
CHAPTER XVIII.
Let no deacon bring a charge of indecency against a presbyter.
CHAPTER XIX.

Let no presbyter, from the day he takes up the charge of the presbyterate, take a wife, so that, even if he has acted in neglect [of this], we say he is deprived of his rank for ten years. But if anyone has acted against this present signed document and public decree, let him be condemned for ever.
CHAPTER XX.

No one shall judge the first see, since all sees desire justice to be tempered by the first see. Neither by the Augustus, nor by all the clergy, nor by kings, nor by the people shall the judge be judged. And two hundred and eighty-four bishops subscribed, and forty-five presbyters, and five deacons, and the two following, and Constantine Augustus, and his mother Helena. And Silvester the bishop fixed this canon in the city of Rome, and sprinkled [it] on all the bishops. Done in the Baths of Trajan, on the third day before the Kalends of June, in the third [consulship] of the Lord Constantine Augustus, and Priscus being consul.
CRITIQUE OF THE FOREGOING CONSTITUTUM.
(Coustant, Appendix, p. 37).

I. This Constitutum survives in an old codex of the Colbert library written in Lombardic capital letters, and in another exemplar of the same library no less ancient, and also in the collection which Baronius, at the year 324, no. 124, calls the Cresconian. Benedict III, and Nicholas I in letter 8 to the emperor Michael, cite it. Petrus Crabbe, having obtained a double very old exemplar of it, presented a triple edition in three columns set side by side. 'Namely, on account of the intolerable and excessive difference and corruption of the exemplars,' he says, 'so that sometimes what they mean cannot be understood, for that reason the letter of each exemplar has been set down syllable by syllable, with no change made. But between the two a third edition has been placed in the middle, emended by conjectures, and brought back, as far as could be done, to the laws of grammar.' Later editors then suppressed this, as being of no authority, content to keep the double one; but at the same time all agree that each in many places, because of the corruption of the exemplars, can either scarcely or not at all be understood. And according to Baronius, no. 123, one can scarcely find a line into which an error has not crept. Yet the venerable name of Silvester so imposed upon each [editor] that, moved by respect for antiquity, they made it a matter of conscience to change almost any letter, even in the more obscure places. But this fault of barbarous speech, alien to common understanding, which this Constitutum shares with the two letters that follow, may rightly seem attributable not so much to the corruption of the exemplars as to the ignorance of the man who forged these writings. Although we would not deny that the copyists too, because of that unusual barbarism of language, while striving to wipe away errors, perhaps admitted new ones, or certainly departed again and again from the fidelity of the archetype. Hence arose those differences of the exemplars, for the display of which a double edition at first seemed necessary. We, however, have thought it enough to note those variants in the margin at their places. But even that inelegance of language alone removes all credibility from a writing to which not only so many bishops and other distinguished men, but also a most learned and most cultivated emperor, are pretended to have subscribed.

II. But afterwards Labbe, thinking that he should by no means agree with Binius, Baronius and others who accepted this little work, noted opposite the title of this Constitutum: "These twenty chapters, which Isidore wove into his collection, seem to Hincmar and to most learned men to be forged." By these words Labbe undoubtedly points to that [passage] of Hincmar, opusc. 48, no. 21, vol. II, p. 793: "For it is written in a certain sermon, without the name of its compiler, excerpted from the acts of St Silvester, which Isidore, bishop of Seville (he would more truly have said Isidore Mercator), collected together with the letters of the pontiffs of the Roman see from St Clement down to Blessed Gregory, that the same St Silvester decreed that no cleric should dare to bring a charge against a layman, and that a presbyter [should not bring a charge] against a bishop, nor a deacon against a presbyter," etc., as below, chap. 3, as far as "having wives and children and wholly preaching Christ"; with this moreover added immediately after: "Let no one accept the testimony of a cleric against a layman." When Hincmar has set this out, he discloses what he thinks of that excerpted sermon, no. 22, in these words: "How contrary these sayings are to one another, and how different from the holy canons and sacred laws, there is no one who doubts"; and he adds, no. 23: "Wherefore it is not to be believed that the same holy man established such things as (or the like of what) are contained written in the said sermon." Nor is there any other place in which Hincmar rejects the twenty forged chapters.

III. But it is not obscure that in the passage cited it is not the following Constitutum that Hincmar mentions, but another little work, which in Isidore is entitled "Certain excerpts from the synodal acts of St Silvester, pope," and in Labbe, vol. I of the Councils, p. 1542, "Brief epilogue of the following Roman council." For Hincmar mentions not the acts of St Silvester themselves, but a sermon taken or excerpted from the acts of St Silvester. He also notes that that excerpted sermon existed without the name of its compiler or excerptor, just as in Isidore too the excerpts from the synodal acts of St Silvester bear no author's name. Although, since they are ascribed to no one else, Isidore himself may rightly be judged to have made the excerpts. Moreover, the passage mentioned by Hincmar is found complete in these excerpts, both in as many words and in the same order of words; whereas, on the contrary, in the following Constitutum its last words, namely "Let no one accept the testimony of a cleric against a layman," stand twelve chapters away from the preceding ones, which Hincmar joins immediately to them; and the earlier ones, "that no cleric should dare to bring a charge against a layman," you would seek with vain labour in the whole Constitutum.

IV. One may also doubt whether Isidore wove into his collection those twenty chapters which the following Constitutum comprises. They are indeed inserted into it in the old codex of the College of Navarre; but in the Noyon [codex], the Colbert ones, or others older than the Navarre one, they appear nowhere. And indeed it would have been altogether superfluous for Mercator to put together excerpts from those twenty chapters, if he had inserted the chapters themselves into his collection.

V. But although Hincmar saw and noted only those excerpts, yet what he judges about their conflict with the ecclesiastical rules applies equally to the Constitutum itself. Certainly it conflicts with them that, as is related in chap. 1, the presbyters stood behind the seated bishops in the Roman council, and no one sat in it except the bishops. For, as Baronius observed, in the Fourth Council of Carthage, canon 34, it is decreed that a bishop sitting in any place should not allow a presbyter to stand. Nor is there any doubt that this law also held at Rome. For, as Jerome testifies, letter 85 to Evagrius, in the church at Rome (even when bishops are present, as is clear from the following words) "the presbyters sit and the deacons stand." So too in the Council of Elvira we read that the bishops sat together, with twenty-six presbyters also sitting and the deacons standing by. The same was always the practice in Roman councils too. Again, what is prescribed in chap. 2 about the number of witnesses conflicts with the ecclesiastical rules. For, as Hincmar very well remarked, the canons on judging bishops or clerics who fall into some crime exist in vain, if this decree is valid.

VI. And to what purpose is provision made by so many canons that sacred virgins should not be violated, and penalties decreed for those violated, if, as is enacted in chap. 10, a virgin were permitted to be consecrated only in the seventieth year of her age? Surely by this canon that great number of sacred virgins with which the Church has always been adorned would have been removed; and if any had remained, the merit of chastity consecrated at that age would thereafter have been slight. But that another custom prevailed in the Church is proved by the sentence of Syagrius, so vehemently condemned by Ambrose, letter 5, by which he had ordered that a sacred virgin named Indicia, when she was accused of violated chastity, be examined by midwives; it is proved both by the treatise To a Fallen Virgin, by the same Ambrose or by another writer no more recent than he, and by the letter of Basil on the same subject; it is proved again by the books of Ambrose On Virgins to his sister Marcellina, written thirteen years after the death of Liberius, who consecrated her; it is proved too by the order of King Huneric, who commanded the sacred virgins to be gathered together, sending midwives to examine their chastity, and by the impious cry of those shouting to these virgins: "Say that the bishops and your clerics sleep with you"; it is proved, finally, by countless other things for which there would have been no place if no virgin were to be consecrated unless advanced to seventy-two years. But more genuine canons, already mentioned elsewhere, oppose this canon, of which some forbid virgins to be consecrated before the twenty-fifth year of their age, others before the fortieth.

VII. The same Constitutum also conflicts with itself, when in chap. 1 it condemns Callistus as a Sabellian, who held that there is one person of the Trinity, and at the same time as one who separated the Trinity; whereas whoever separates the Trinity follows a heresy opposed to the Sabellian. For this consisted in confounding the Trinity, not in separating it.

VIII. Here, moreover, one is moved to wonder why in so famous an assembly, with Constantine present, in the very year in which the same emperor was applying himself with all zeal to extinguishing the fires of the Arian heresy, and in which he had therefore sent the great Hosius with letters to Alexandria, not even a word is said about Arius, and only Callistus, Jovianus, Hippolytus the deacon, and Victorinus are condemned, names unknown in ecclesiastical records; if indeed this Victorinus is other than Victorius, the composer of the Easter cycles, which we shall consider presently. Nor does the conjecture of Binius or Baronius, who think that the case of Arius was then reserved for the ecumenical Council of Nicaea, sufficiently meet this objection. For it is far more probable that Silvester and Constantine, in the month of May of the year 324, had as yet given no thought to assembling the Council of Nicaea. But suppose they had already decided on it in their minds: what prevented matters to be treated and defined in the ecumenical [council] from being prepared in the Roman assembly? Certainly it was afterwards the custom of the Roman pontiffs to anticipate general councils with synods held at Rome, and to condemn beforehand in the latter the heresies to be condemned in the former. Besides, it is not easy to guess how fifty-seven bishops of the region and of Rhinocorura are listed; and it is harder to understand for what reason so many Egyptian prelates had then come together to Silvester, unless to complain of the perverse doctrine of Arius and the crimes of the Arians, or how they could have allowed silence to be kept on so grave and so necessary a matter.

IX. To whom, too, would there not seem suspect, in the catalogue of Greek bishops, so many purely Latin names, for example Quodvultdeus, Spesindeo, Exsuperantius, Exitiosus, Fortunatus, Potestas, Sempervivus, etc.? For although Latins sometimes borrow names from the Greeks, yet the Greeks do not commonly do so.

X. The discourse would run on too long if we pursued one by one all the marks of falsity that occur in the work we are examining. Its forgery is proved more than enough from the very opening by the fabulous story of Constantine's leprosy and its cure, and the faulty consular dating at the end confirms it as if with a seal.

XI. Moreover, from the aforesaid mention of Constantine's leprosy and of his baptism conferred by Silvester, it follows that the following Constitutum is more recent than the false Acts of Silvester. At least it cannot be denied that those false Acts of Silvester were known to the architect of this Constitutum, inasmuch as he drew from them the said fable about the leprosy and baptism of Constantine. On the other hand, from what Hincmar long ago observed (Hincm. opusc. 48, no. 23, p. 792), namely that nothing at all is read in the Acts of Silvester similar to what we meet in the Constitutum, or in the excerpts agreeing with that Constitutum, but that these things are mentioned only in the books of the pontiffs, we may rightly conclude that the said Constitutum and the pseudo-Roman council were unknown to the author of those Acts. For who could persuade himself that he would have passed over so celebrated an event in silence in those Acts?

XII. When we have also examined who that Victorinus is whose condemnation is demanded in chapter 1 because he 'asserted to people whatever he wished' and 'declared the paschal cycles false', another argument will be supplied to us from this, by which we may confirm that this Constitutum is much more recent than the times of Silvester. And first, in passing, we observe that the same Victorinus is likewise blamed in the following letter 13 because 'by his own judgement he asserted whatever he wished, and declared the cycles of Easter false', so that everyone may notice in advance from what source this little stream also flowed. Now, to one who investigates who that Victorinus is who is blamed in both writings on account of new Easter cycles, no other will present himself than Victorinus of Aquitaine, called Victorius by most and Victor by some, who in the year of Christ 457, at the request of Hilarus, then archdeacon and afterwards pope, composed Easter cycles. For although Pope Leo approved these cycles, and the Fourth Synod of Orléans, held in the year 541, admitted them in canon 1, yet many afterwards rejected them and sharply criticised them. In particular, Victor, bishop of Capua, in the year 550 wrote a book against Victorius himself, in the course of which, as Bede attests (Bede, On the Reckoning of Time, ch. 40), he spoke thus: 'Now, I say, order requires that I lay open the errors of the cycles which Victorius published, since he does not know how to determine the lawful Easter day.' How little better Columbanus thought of the same cycles at the end of the sixth century, his own letter written to Pope Gregory I (Greg. book III, letter 132 in the new edition) attests in these words: 'For know that by our masters and the ancient Irish philosophers, and the most learned computists in composing the reckoning, Victorius has not been received, but rather [is held] worthy of laughter or pardon than of authority.' And after some intervening words he adds: 'Therefore either excuse or condemn your Victorius.' And the rest of the letter gives proof of how much the Irish shrank from the reckoning of Victorius. Nor were the Western Britons more favourably disposed towards him. For these, as Aldhelm writes in the letters of St Boniface, letter 44, 'decreed that the course of Victorius's paschal table was not to be followed by posterity.'

XIII. Nor should anyone be troubled by the fact that, although many have written about Victorius, who drew up paschal cycles in the times of Pope Leo, for example Gennadius of Marseilles, Isidore of Seville, Gregory of Tours, Fredegar, Aldhelm, Honorius of Autun, etc., yet not one of them calls him a bishop; whereas the Victorinus mentioned in the Constitutum of Silvester is called bishop more than once. For it is certain from the cited words of Columbanus to Gregory, 'Therefore either excuse or condemn your Victorius', that Columbanus is censuring the Victorius whose cycles Rome had received and was still then following, and hence that very Victorius who had composed the cycles in Leo's times. And that this Victorius was a bishop the same Columbanus reveals, in the same letter, that he had no doubt at all, where he says: 'It does not satisfy me, after so many authors whom I have read, [to have] a single opinion of these bishops, who say only: We must not keep Easter with the Jews. BISHOP VICTOR once said this, but none of the Easterners accepted the fabrication.' For anyone who has examined what precedes and what follows will not doubt that here is mentioned not Victor, bishop of Capua, but Victorius himself, who is vehemently attacked throughout the letter. And indeed, as we have said, the one who is called Victorius by most is named Victorinus by Isidore (Etymologies book VI, ch. 17) and Victor by Fredegar (ch. 108). Concerning the episcopate, then, of the Victorius whose cycles Rome received, let each think what he pleases. Certainly it is no further from the truth that he could have been believed a bishop by the architect of this Constitutum than [that he was so believed] by Columbanus and others who rejected that same cycle not without indignation. And if this is so, no one can deny that this Constitutum is not later than the middle of the sixth century. By another argument we have already proved, in the general preface § 3, that it fits the times of Pope Symmachus.
MENTION
OF ANOTHER ROMAN COUNCIL WHICH WAS ALSO HELD AT ROME UNDER POPE SILVESTER,
TWO [YEARS] BEFORE THE FOREGOING.
(Councils vol. I, col. 1490, Labbe's edition.)

In this council at Rome, in the presence of the emperor Constantine, that most celebrated disputation between the Jews and Silvester was held, for which, at the instance of the emperor and of his mother Helena, very learned men of both sides came together with this aim, that the defenders of each party should prove and make manifest the truth of their religion by scriptures and miracles alike. Concerning its outcome, the Acts of Silvester are found cited in these words in the third letter written by Hadrian, the Roman pontiff, to Charlemagne: 'In the very beginnings of the Christians, when the emperor Constantine was being converted to the faith, his mother Helena Augusta came to him in the city of Rome with twelve scribes and Pharisees, and teachers and leaders of the Jews; and she, together with her son Constantine Augustus, decreed that the Jews should hold a council with the Christians. In it the holy Pope Silvester presided with very many most holy bishops, and, extending the faith of the Christians to a wider state, they were made victors, both through sacred scripture and through miracles, under the Lord's protection (by the judgement of Crato the philosopher and Zenophilus, a man of senatorial rank, whom they had chosen for this).' The Acts of Silvester [tell] these things at greater length; their authority before Gelasius was so great that they were read both at Rome and in many other churches; indeed even after Gelasius they were cited as if authentic by Pope Hadrian in the aforesaid letter 3 to Charlemagne. But as they exist today, they teem with many lies which had crept in from elsewhere. For what they report, that Constantine was a Christian before Helena; that Constantius and Constans, Caesars and Augusti, were living in the East at this time; that Isaac held the high priesthood among the Jews; that Helena was a native of Bithynia; that the Saturday fast was abolished by Silvester; that Sunday was instituted by him; that Silvester himself was ordained pontiff by Miltiades; and many other things, are wholly foreign to the truth, as, besides Baronius showing it admirably at the year 315, no. 12 and following, the canons of the apostles themselves and the notes we have written there also plainly demonstrate.

That this assembly was held when Constantine and Licinius were holding their fourth consulship, namely in the year of Christ 315, which is the second of Silvester and the tenth of Constantine, is attested by the Acts of Silvester and by law 1 on the Jews in the Theodosian Code, dated under these consuls. For when, confounded by this disputation, they not only inflicted insults and grave injuries on the Christians but even stirred up sedition against the emperor himself, [Constantine], to ward off injury from the heads of the Christians, by the said law promulgated against them, decreed that if they harassed any Christian deserter from their sect with stones or any other savage punishment, they should immediately be given to the flames. And to suppress their rebellion and sedition, he had the seditious, with their ears cut off and a mark branded on their bodies, led around through all places like runaway slaves and rogues deserving the lash. Chrysostom, discourse against the Jews, homily 2; Baronius, at the aforesaid year, nos. 9 and 10.
Critique of the following letter.
(Coustant, Appendix, p. 35.)

I. Letter VII, forged in the name of Cornelius, is followed in the library of Fleury by the next [letter], of no greater authority. For it consists of the same words as letter I of Pope Zosimus, with the names Vienne and Paschasius substituted in place of the words Arles and Patroclus, and, in place of what Zosimus explains in chapters 1 and 2, with the addition of what is contained in no. 2. Either, then, this [letter] of Silvester or that of Zosimus must be called false. But the genuineness of letter I of Zosimus is proved not only by two other [letters] of the same pontiff, namely the seventh and the tenth, in which the same right of granting formatae [letters of communion] is asserted for Patroclus, bishop of Arles, but also several others confirm [it] for the successors of Zosimus towards the successors of Patroclus. For we still have letters of Pope Symmachus and of Vigilius, in which they attest that they granted this right, after the custom of their predecessors, to Caesarius, Auxanius and Aurelian, bishops of Arles. The architect of another letter of Zosimus, to Simplicius, bishop of Vienne, to be appended below in its place, whom we suspect to be no other than the fabricator of this very [letter], freely admits the genuineness of the letters written by Zosimus in favour of the bishop of Arles. Indeed, he supposes this [letter] of Silvester unknown to this pope, whereas Zosimus could not have copied it unless he had had it before his eyes. And indeed, when we compare these words of Zosimus's letter I, 'This privilege of formatae we have granted to our brother and fellow bishop Patroclus in special consideration of his merits', with these of the letter of Silvester, 'This privilege of formatae we have granted to our brother and fellow bishop Paschasius AND TO HIS POSTERITY in special consideration of his merits', we catch there not Zosimus copying Silvester's words, but pseudo-Silvester clumsily interpolating Zosimus's statement. For what does this 'and to his posterity' mean? Was this said of Paschasius's children and grandchildren? Silvester would surely have said 'and to his successors'. But neither should he have said 'in special consideration of his merits', if he had wished the same privilege to extend to Paschasius's successors. We pass over the fact that none of his successors is read to have used it; that in the controversy which flared up with such partisan zeal between the church of Arles and that of Vienne over the privileges of their sees, it never occurred to any bishop, whether of Rome or of Vienne, to mention this letter of Silvester; that Zosimus, in bestowing the privilege of formatae on Patroclus, speaks as though he knew for certain that it had been granted to no one in Gaul before; and finally that the same privilege is established to have been granted to other successors of Patroclus.

II. Moreover, in a codex of canons written more than 800 years ago, which the celebrated monastery of Murbach in the diocese of Basel preserves, we read inserted a privilege, or part of a privilege, with this title: 'Here begins the constitution of the apostolic see. Silvester, bishop, to all the bishops throughout the Gauls and the seven provinces.' Then there is appended the whole of chapter 1 of the first letter of Pope Zosimus, except that in this codex 'metropolitan of Autun' has been substituted for 'metropolitan of Arles', and Reticius for Patroclus. But we never read that the title of metropolitan was granted to the bishop of Autun, still less in the age of Reticius. For Gregory, after he granted Syagrius the use of the pallium, wished him to regard this as a very great favour, for 'this too', he says, 'we have likewise seen fit to grant: that, the place and honour of his metropolitan being preserved in all respects, the church of the city of Autun... should rank after the church of Lyon, and should claim this place and rank for itself by the indulgence of our authority.' Hence it appears to have happened more than once that those who sought to convince others of the antiquity of some church's privileges set before themselves, as a model to imitate, the privilege granted by Zosimus to Patroclus. Further, the Murbach codex itself proves the integrity of that privilege, since after its first chapter, adapted in the manner we have described to Pope Silvester and Reticius of Autun, it appends the remaining two chapters of Zosimus's letter, ascribed no longer to Reticius, but to Zosimus himself, or, as it is corruptly written there, 'Ozimus'.
LETTER
ON RECEIVING FORMATAE FROM THE BISHOP OF VIENNE. WHICH ARE THE SEVEN PROVINCES BELONGING TO THE CHURCH OF VIENNE.
(From the same source.)
Pope Silvester to all the bishops throughout the Gauls and throughout the seven provinces.

1. It has pleased the apostolic see that if anyone from any part of the Gauls, of whatever ecclesiastical rank, seeks to come to us, or plans to go to other places in the world, he should not set out unless he has received formatae from the metropolitan of Vienne, by which his priesthood or the ecclesiastical position he holds may be made clear through the attestation of his writings. We have decreed this for the reason that very many, pretending to be bishops, priests or clerics, creep into a name worthy of veneration, because there exists no document of formatae by which they can be refuted, and thereby obtain veneration that is not owed them. Whoever, therefore, dearest brothers, whether he be bishop, priest or deacon, or set in a lower rank, comes to us henceforth without the aforesaid formata, let him know that he cannot be received at all. It is clear that we have sent this authoritative ruling everywhere, so that it may become known in all these regions that what we have decreed is to be observed in every way. But if anyone presumes of his own accord to violate these salutary decrees, let him know that he is cut off from our communion. This privilege of formatae we have granted to [our] brother and fellow bishop Paschasius and to his posterity, in special consideration of his merits.

2. The seven provinces belonging to the church of Vienne, as the Roman catalogue testifies, are these: Viennensis, first; Narbonensis Prima, which is second; Narbonensis Secunda, which is Aix, third; Aquitanica Prima, which is Bourges, fourth; Aquitanica Secunda, which is Bordeaux (add: fifth); Novempopulana, which is Auch, sixth; and the Maritime Alps, which is Embrun, seventh. Farewell.
